It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "People will be gathered naked and barefoot." Umm Salamah said: "What about the women?" He said: "The people will be occupied, O Umm Salamah." She said: "And what will occupy them?" He said: "The spreading of the pages, in which are the weights of the atoms and the weights of the mustard seed." [Al-Tha'labi related it through Muhammad ibn Abi Musa from 'Ata' ibn Yasar from Umm Salamah with this wording. Its origin is in the two Sahihs from 'A'ishah, and al-Hakim related it from the hadith of Sawdah.] It is possible that what is meant is: "they were spread among their owners," that is, they were separated among them. It is related from Murthid ibn Wada'ah: when the Day of Resurrection comes, the pages will fly from beneath the Throne. The believer's page will fall into his hand in a lofty Garden, and the disbeliever's page will fall into his hand amid scorching wind and boiling water. That is, that is written in them. These are pages other than the pages of deeds.

﴿When the sky is stripped away﴾ [Qur'an 81:11]. *Kushitat*: it is uncovered and removed, as the hide is stripped from the slaughtered animal, and the covering from a thing. Ibn Mas'ud read *qushitat* (with a qaf). The interchange of *kaf* and *qaf* is common: one says *labakat al-tharid* and *labaqat*, and *al-kafur* and *al-qafur*.

﴿When Hell is kindled﴾ [Qur'an 81:12]. *Su'irat* or *quddat* means kindled with intense kindling. It is read *su''irat* with the doubled form for emphasis. It was said: its kindling is the anger of Allah the Exalted and the sins of the children of Adam.

﴿When Paradise is brought near﴾ [Qur'an 81:13]. *Uzlifat* means brought near to the God-fearing, as in His saying: ﴿and Paradise is brought near for the God-fearing, not far away﴾ [Qur'an 50:31]. It was said: these are twelve characteristics, six of which are in this world and six in the Hereafter.

*'Alimat* is the operator of the accusative in *idha al-shamsu kuwwirat* and in what is conjoined to it. If you ask: every soul knows what it has brought forth, as in His saying: ﴿on the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ [Qur'an 3:30], not one soul alone. So what is the meaning of His saying *'alimat nafs* (a soul has known)? I say: this is from the reverse of their speech, by which they intend exaggeration in what is described by the reverse. From it is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Those who disbelieved will often wish they had been Muslims﴾ [Qur'an 15:2]. Its meaning is the meaning of *kam* (how many), and more emphatic than it. The saying of the speaker:

*Qad atruku al-qarna musfarran anamiluhu* [This verse's explanation was given in the first volume, page 202, so refer to it if you wish.]

You say to one of the commanders of the armies: "How many horsemen do you have?" He says: "Many a horseman I have," or: "you will not lack a horseman with me," and with him are the *maqani* [a *maqnab* in al-Sihah is what is between thirty and forty horses]. His intention by this is continuing to increase the number of his horsemen, but he intended to show his innocence of exaggeration, and that he is one who minimizes what he has, let alone exaggerates. So he used the wording of minimization, and from it the meaning of abundance is understood with correctness and certainty. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that a reciter recited it in his presence, and when he reached *'alimat nafs ma ahdarat*, he said: "And my back is broken."

Meccan, and its verses are 29 [revealed after Surah al-Masad]. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Regarding *al-takwir* (the folding up, wrapping) there are two interpretations. It may come from *kawwarat al-'imamah*, "I wrapped the turban" when I wound it. The meaning is that its light is wound up, so its spreading and dispersal across the horizons ends. This is an expression for removing it and taking it away, because as long as it remains, its light is spread out and not wound up. Or its wrapping may be an expression for raising it and covering it, because when a garment is to be lifted, it is folded and rolled up. Similar to this is His saying, ﴿On the Day We will roll up the heavens﴾ [Qur'an 21:104]. Or it may come from *tawwara* and *kawwara*, "he struck him and threw him down," meaning he cast it, that is, it is hurled and thrown out of its orbit, just as the stars are described as *inkidar* (falling). If you ask: is the *ash-shams* (the sun) in the nominative as a subject or as an agent? I say: it is in the nominative as an agent, raised by a hidden verb that *kuwwirat* explains, because *idha* (when) requires a verb, owing to the conditional meaning it carries. *Inkadarat* means "fell down, came to an end." The poet said:

*Absara kharban fada'in fankadar*
*Idha al-kirami btadaru al-ba'a badr*
*Taqaddi al-bazi idha al-bazi kasar*
*Anna janahayhi min al-tawdi famar*

[Al-'Ajjaj praises 'Umar ibn 'Ubayd Allah al-Tamimi. *Al-ba'* with an unpointed initial letter is the measure of the stretch of the two arms, and the intended meaning is generosity, metaphorically. *Badr* means he hastened and outdid the generous. *Taqaddi* is in the accusative governed by it; its original form was *taqadadda*, the second letter was replaced by a weak letter and the first was given a kasra. That is, he inclined his two wings and brought them near the great mountain, and *marr* means he went along the face of the mountain. *Kharban* is the plural of *kharb*, a bird called the bustard, and it is in construction with *fada'* (open space). *Fankadar* means he swooped down and fell upon them, and so devoured them. The beginning of this verse is also related:]

*Laqad sama ibn Ma'mar hina i'tamar*
*Maghza ba'idan min ba'idin wa dabar*

[*I'tamar* means he visited. *Al-maghza* is the place of raiding. *Dabarahu dabran* means he gathered it together. He says: his rank rose when he raided a distant place from Syria and gathered a great army for that, and he hastened like the falcon's swoop upon the bustard. He exaggerated in describing the falcon, to portray the situation of the one compared, and as an exaggeration in praising him.]

It is related regarding the sun and the stars that they will be cast into Hell so that those who worshipped them may see them, as He said: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾ [Qur'an 21:98]. *Suyyirat* means: on the face of the earth and removed far away. Or they will be moved through the air, moving like clouds, as in His saying: ﴿while they pass as the passing of clouds﴾ [Qur'an 27:88]. *Al-'ishar* is the plural of *'ishra'*, as *al-nifas* is the plural of *nafsa'*. It is the she-camel that has passed ten months of pregnancy, and then it is called by this name until it gives birth, completing the year. It is the most precious of things to its owners and the dearest to them. *'Uttilat* means left abandoned and neglected. It was said: its owners neglected it from milking and suckling because they were busy with themselves. It is also read *'uttilat* with the lighter form. *Hushirat* means gathered from every side. Qatadah said: every creature will be gathered, even the flies, for retribution. It was also said: when judgment is passed between them, they will be turned to dust, so nothing will remain of them except what gives joy to the children of Adam and pleases them with its form, such as the peacock and the like. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that *hashruha* means their death. It is said: when drought oppresses the people and their wealth, the drought gathers them. It is also read *hushirat* with the doubled form. *Sujjirat*: it is read with both the light and the doubled forms, from *sajjara al-tannur*, when one fills the oven with firewood. That is, they are filled, and some of them are made to surge into others until they become one sea. It was said: they are filled with flaming fires to torment the people of the Fire. It is related from al-Hasan: their water will go away, and no drop will remain in them. *Zuwwijat* means each soul is joined to its like. It was said: souls are joined to bodies. It was said: they are joined to their books and deeds. It is related from al-Hasan: it is like His saying: ﴿And you will be in three kinds﴾ [Qur'an 56:7]. It was said: the souls of the believers are joined to the houris, and the souls of the disbelievers to the devils.

*Ada' yi'idu* is reversed from *ada' ya'udu*, meaning to burden. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and their preservation does not burden Him﴾ [Qur'an 2:255]. It is because it is a burdening with dust. A man, when a daughter was born to him and he wished to keep her alive, would dress her in a garment of wool or hair, and she would graze for him the camels and sheep in the desert. If he wished to kill her, he would leave her until she was six years old, and then he would say to her mother: perfume her and adorn her, so that I may take her to her in-laws. He would have dug a well for her in the desert, and he would bring her to the well and say to her: look into it. Then he would push her from behind and cover her with earth until the well was level with the ground. It was also said: when a pregnant woman was near her delivery, she would dig a pit and labour at its edge. If she gave birth to a daughter, she threw her into the pit, and if she gave birth to a son, she kept him. If you ask: what moved them to bury the daughters alive? They used to say that the angels are the daughters of Allah, so they attributed the daughters to Him, and He had more right to them. Sa'sa'ah ibn Najiyah was among those who prohibited burying alive, and al-Farazdaq boasted of this in his saying:

*Wa minna alladhi mana' al-wa'idat*
*Fa-ahya al-wa'id fa-lam tu'ad*

[Al-Farazdaq boasts of his grandfather Sa'sa'ah. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), accepted Islam, and said: O Messenger of Allah, I did deeds in the Jahiliyyah; is there any reward for them? He said: What did you do? He said: I saved sixty-three girls from being buried alive, buying each one for two she-camels of ten months and a male camel. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: This is from the category of righteousness, and you have its reward, since Allah has bestowed upon you Islam. It is said: "He buried his daughter" when he buried her while she was alive. The tribe of Kindah used to do this out of fear of shame and poverty. It is related: *fa-ahya al-wa'id wa-hiya awqa'* (and this is more forceful). *Al-wa'id* is said of the singular and the plural, masculine or feminine. It is related: *wa-jaddi*, that is, he is the one who prevented the groups who buried their daughters alive, and he ransomed them from death, so it is as if he gave them life. The word *al-wa'id* is used metaphorically for those who are about to die, and the "giving life" is an embellishment.]

If you ask: what is the meaning of asking the buried girl about the sin for which she was killed? Why was the one who buried her not asked about the reason for killing her? I say: her questioning and her answer are a rebuke to her killer, similar to the rebuke in His saying to 'Isa (Jesus): ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾ [Qur'an 5:116]. It is read *su'ilat* (she was asked), meaning she disputed on her own behalf, and asked Allah or her killer. The phrase *qutilat* is used because the speech is a report about her. If the words addressed to her when she was asked were quoted, it would be said: "you were killed." Or, if her speech when she was asked were quoted, it would be said: "you were killed." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) read *qutilat* as a quotation. It is also read *qutillat* with the doubled form. In this there is clear evidence that the children of polytheists are not punished, and that punishment is deserved only for a sin. When Allah rebukes the disbeliever with the innocence of the buried girl from any sin, how evil is he (the disbeliever), who does not wrong even the weight of an atom, if He then turns against her after this rebuke and does to her what she forgets from the perpetrator of the rebuke, namely the severe and everlasting punishment. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he was asked about this and he argued with this verse.

بِالْخُنَّسِ: the ones that recede, the retrogrades. For example, you see a star at the end of a zodiacal sign, and then it turns back and returns to the start of that sign.

﴿وَالْجَوارِ﴾: the ones that run, the planets.

﴿الْكُنَّسِ﴾: the ones that hide, from the verb *kanasa* (said of a wild animal when it enters its lair, *kunās*).

It is said that these are the five wandering stars: Bahram [[Note on "Bahram": it is not Arabic, and it refers to Mars (al-Marrikh). (ʿ)]], Zuhal (Saturn), ʿUtarid (Mercury), al-Zuhra (Venus), and al-Mushtari (Jupiter). They move with the sun and the moon, then turn back until they are hidden beneath the light of the sun. Their *khunūs* is their retrogression, and their *kunūs* is their concealment beneath the light of the sun.

It is also said that these are all the stars: they recede by day and so vanish from sight, and they hide by night, that is, they rise in their places, like wild beasts in their lairs.

ʿAssaʿsa al-layl and saʿsaʿa: when the night turns its back (i.e., withdraws). Al-ʿAjjaj said:

*"Until, when the dawn breathed for her, and her night was withdrawn from her and turned away."*

[[Al-ʿAjjaj. *Tanaffus al-ṣubḥ* means the spreading of its light, or its advance with light and a breeze. The pronoun in *"lahā"* refers to the sun. It is also said that it refers to the desert (*mafāza*). *Injāba* means that the darkness of the night was cut off and separated from her. *ʿAssaʿsa* means it turned away and retreated, and its darkness departed; so it is an emphasis of what precedes it. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to a wild cow, for example.]]

It is also said: *ʿAssaʿsa* means that its darkness advances (*iqbāl*). If you ask: what is the meaning of the dawn's *tanaffus*? I answer: when the dawn advances, a spirit and a breeze advance with its advance, so this is made a breath for it, by way of metaphor. It is also said: *tanaffusa al-ṣubḥ* (the dawn breathed).

[[The author of the commentary has dealt with the issue of *ʿaṭf ʿalā ʿāmilayn* (conjoining with two governing elements) in his commentary on Sūrat al-Takwīr. Shaykh Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥājib (Ibn al-Ḥājib) adopted the permissibility of conjoining over two governing elements, and took this verse as his support and proof in opposing Sībawayh. He refuted al-Zamakhsharī's answer in his commentary on Sūrat al-Shams (*wa-l-shams wa-ḍuḥāhā*), because the answer did not hold consistently here. Had he reflected on his refutation, he would have praised the sharpness of al-Zamakhsharī's insight in deriving it. We, with God's help and guidance, adopt the position of Sībawayh that it is impossible to conjoin over two governing elements by making the second waw a conjunction. The answer of al-Zamakhsharī holds here and can be applied to this verse, as follows: Regarding God's words *"wa-l-layli idhā ʿassaʿas"*, this first waw is the beginning of a new oath (*ibtidāʾ qasam*, an independent oath), and the waw in His words *"wa-l-ṣubḥi idhā tanaffas"* is a conjunction (*ʿāṭifa*), so al-Zamakhsharī's answer holds consistently.

If it is said: You have contradicted Sībawayh, for he does not regard a waw that follows an oath as an independent oath, but as a conjunction, and you have made the first waw, which follows the oath, an independent oath. We reply: Sībawayh spoke about a waw that follows an oath introduced by waw. As for this verse, the first oath in it is introduced by *bāʾ* and a verb, so we took the following waw as a secondary and subordinate oath, and this is more eloquent, as if He swore two oaths by two different things. If it is said: Yes, Sībawayh spoke about the waw following an oath introduced by waw; so what is the difference between a waw following an oath introduced by waw and one following an oath introduced by *bāʾ*? They are only the same, for each of them is an instrument of the oath, and the *tāʾ* indicates the *bāʾ*, so their ruling is one. We reply: They are not the same, for when the oath begins with waw and no other waw follows it, making it another oath entails repetition that is disliked, since the instrument is one. This is not the case when the instrument differs, for then the risk of repetition is absent. Do you not see that if the oath began with waw and then an oath with *bāʾ* followed it, it would be necessary to regard them as two independent oaths? The same would apply if this order were reversed.

Also, if what prevents Sībawayh from regarding the second waw as an independent oath is that the answer is single and the first waw requires an omitted element, then conjunction dispenses with the need to assume an omitted element, so it becomes the necessary reading. The *bāʾ* does not imply a repetition, because it is the origin of the oath, especially with the explicit mention of the oath-verb and its reinforcement by the addition of *lā*. In all this there is what suffices without a separate stated answer. This is not the case with the waw, for its capacity in the oath is weak compared with the *bāʾ*. So the omission of an answer whose indication is firmly established does not require the omission of an answer less clear than it.

I end the discussion of this question with a wonderful point. I specified the objection to the second waw, in His words *"wa-l-layli idhā ʿassaʿas"*, rather than the third, because it does not apply to the third. Do you not see that if you made it a conjunction, you would not be obliged to conjoin over two governing elements? For we would make it stand in place of the *bāʾ*, and make *idhā* in it governed directly by the verb, provided no adverbial element precedes it in the verbal clause on which *idhā* could be conjoined. It becomes like your saying: *"I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr today."* Here *al-yawm* is governed directly by the verb, and it is understood from the example that your passing by Zayd is unrestricted, not limited by a time expression; the restriction to *al-yawm* applies only to your passing by ʿAmr. This accords with the verse, for although the verb governs the adverbial element directly, that element restricts the oath to the night, not to the oath by the *khunnas*.]]

The Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 81, verses 19–21:

﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. The "noble messenger" is Jibril (Gabriel), upon him be blessings from God.

[[Mahmud said: "By the noble messenger is meant Jibril, peace be upon him. His saying, ﴿with the Lord of the Throne﴾, indicates the greatness of his rank and station. And 'thumma' (there) is a reference to the aforementioned location, meaning 'with the Lord of the Throne', etc."

Ahmad said: Jibril, upon him be blessings from God, would not have approved of this interpretation, which contains a deficiency in regard to the bearer of good news and warner, upon him be the best of prayers and peace. Al-Zamakhshari has followed his own desire in establishing the foundations of his corrupt school, and he has erred both in the root and in the branch. We will clarify this, by God's power and strength, and say:

First: the exegetes (ahl al-tafsir) have differed. A great multitude among them held that the meaning of "the noble messenger" here, through to the end of the attributes, is Muhammad ﷺ. If that is so, and God knows best, then it is the customary grace of God upon His Prophet. If the intended one is Jibril, peace be upon him, then people have differed over the preference between angels and messengers. The well-known view of Abu al-Hasan is the preference of messengers, while the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that holds the angels are superior) is the preference of angels. However, the disputants agreed that it is not permissible to prefer one of the two noble categories in a way that implies the disparagement of a specific angel or a specific messenger, because although preference in general is established, specifying it causes harm to the one who is deemed inferior. On this basis the skilled scholars interpreted his saying ﷺ, "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta," meaning: do not specify a lesser one by name. For the general preference is established by the consensus of the Muslims, namely the preference of the Prophet ﷺ over all the prophets.

My grandfather, may God have mercy upon him, used to clarify this with an example. He would say: if you were to say in the presence of a group of jurists, "So-and-so is the most excellent of the people of his age," there would be room within the group for this preference, even though it necessarily includes them among the inferior ones. But if you specified one of them and said, "So-and-so is better than you and more God-fearing," the harm would quickly reach some of you.

When it has been established for you that belief in general preference does not necessarily entail the permissibility of specific preference, you will know that al-Zamakhshari erred according to his own principle. For even if the angels were superior, as he believes, it would not be permissible to say that a specific angel is superior to a specific prophet, especially regarding the master of the children of Adam, upon him be the best of prayers and peace.

Then the discussion returns to the verse, after granting that the intended one is Jibril, and after we leave to God the matter of his specifying the Prophet ﷺ and considering him inferior. We say: no attribute is mentioned in it except that the Prophet ﷺ shares it. The first of them is "noble messenger," and it has been said of him ﷺ at the end of Surat al-Haqqah: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾. It has also been said that the intended one is Jibril, except that the verse ﴿and it is not the word of a poet﴾ rejects this. Al-Zamakhshari agreed with this earlier. This is the first of the attributes and the greatest of them.

As for His saying ﴿possessor of power﴾, it is not the point of disagreement, since there is no dispute that Jibril, peace be upon him, has the superiority of physical strength, and that he can uproot cities with a feather of his wing. There is no doubt about the superiority of his strength over human strength. This has been said in the interpretation of His saying ﴿possessor of strength, and he stood poised﴾. And His saying ﴿with the Lord of the Throne, one firmly established, obeyed, and trustworthy there﴾: the obedience of the angels to our Prophet ﷺ is also established. It is reported that Jibril, peace be upon him, said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Indeed God sends you His greeting." And when Quraysh harmed him, God commanded the angel of the mountains to obey him. The angel greeted him and said, "If you command me, I will bring the two Akhshabs down upon them." But the Prophet ﷺ was patient and sought his reward from God.

Greater than that and more noble is his praised station in the great intercession, on the Day when no one will precede him, when God, exalted is He, says to him: "Raise your head, speak and you will be heard, ask and you will be given, intercede and your intercession will be accepted." As for "trustworthy," he has said, and he is the truthful and the one whose truthfulness is confirmed: "By God, I am trustworthy on earth and trustworthy in heaven." And sufficient for you is His saying: ﴿and he is not accused regarding the unseen﴾. If one reads it with the letter ẓāʾ (ẓanīn), its meaning is that he ﷺ is trustworthy regarding the unseen, not suspected. If one reads it with the letter ḍād (ḍanīn), it returns to generosity. How then can one go to preference by attributes shared equally between the superior and the inferior? I have no discussion concerning the root of the question, but the refutation of his error in every statement is necessary. Otherwise, the question belongs to a different book. So we ask God to make us steadfast in faith in Him, His angels, His books and His messengers, and in the firm word in this world and the Hereafter, and to fill our hearts with love for them, and to make our seeking of nearness to Him through them. He is sufficient for us and the best Disposer of affairs.]]

We say: no attribute is mentioned in it except that the Prophet ﷺ shares it. This is the first of the attributes and the greatest of them.

As for His saying ﴿possessor of power﴾, it is not the point of disagreement, since there is no dispute that Jibril, peace be upon him, has the superiority of physical strength, and that he can uproot cities with a feather of his wing. There is no doubt about the superiority of his strength over human strength. This has been said in the interpretation of His saying ﴿possessor of strength, and he stood poised﴾. And His saying ﴿with the Lord of the Throne, one firmly established, obeyed, and trustworthy there﴾: the obedience of the angels to our Prophet ﷺ is also established. It is reported that Jibril, peace be upon him, said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Indeed God sends you His greeting." And when Quraysh harmed him, God commanded the angel of the mountains to obey him. The angel greeted him and said, "If you command me, I will bring the two Akhshabs down upon them." But the Prophet ﷺ was patient and sought his reward from God.

I have no discussion concerning the root of the question, but the refutation of his error in every statement is necessary. Otherwise, the question belongs to a different book. So we ask God to make us steadfast in faith in Him, His angels, His books and His messengers, and in the firm word in this world and the Hereafter, and to fill our hearts with love for them, and to make our seeking of nearness to Him through them. He is sufficient for us and the best Disposer of affairs.]]

﴿Possessor of power﴾ is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿mighty in strength﴾ and ﴿possessor of firm strength﴾. Since the status of a station follows the status of the one who possesses it, he said:

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 81, verses 23–25:

﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon.﴾ That is, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril (Gabriel) on the clear horizon, at the rising place of the sun, the highest point. ﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen.﴾ That is, Muhammad is not accused (bi-muttaham) of withholding what he reports of the unseen, such as the vision of Jibril, the revelation to him, and other things. Dannin (stingy) here means "accused" (muttaham), from the word al-zunna, which is accusation. It has also been read as bi-ḍanīn, from al-ḍann, which means miserliness; that is, he does not withhold the revelation so that he hides part of it and does not convey it, nor does he refuse to teach when asked to teach, so he does not teach. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it is written with the letter ẓāʾ (ظ), and in the codex of Ubayy with the letter ḍād (ض). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite with both.

Mastering the distinction between the letters ḍād and ẓāʾ is obligatory. Knowing their points of articulation is indispensable for the reciter, for most non-Arabs do not distinguish between the two letters, and even when they do, they distinguish them incorrectly, while there is a great difference between them. The point of articulation of the ḍād (ض) is from the root of the edge of the tongue and what is adjacent to it of the molars, from the right or left side of the tongue. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) was most precise in this; he would use both hands and would articulate the ḍād from both sides of his tongue. It is one of the shajariyya letters (the letters articulated from the side of the tongue), the sister of jīm and shīn. As for the ẓāʾ (ظ), its point of articulation is from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the upper incisors, and it is one of the dhawlaqiyya letters (articulated from the tip of the tongue), the sister of dhāl and thāʾ. If the two letters were identical, two readings would not have been established in this word, nor a difference between two mountains of knowledge and recitation, and the meaning, derivation and structure would not have differed. If you say: what if the reciter substitutes one of the two letters for the other? I say: that is like someone who puts dhāl in place of jīm and thāʾ in place of shīn, because the difference between ḍād and ẓāʾ is like the difference between their sisters.

﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil.﴾ That is, the Qur'an is not the word of some of the eavesdroppers on the heavens (al-mustarziqa lil-sam‘), nor their revelation to their allies among the soothsayers (al-kahana).

فَأَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ﴾ ﴿Istidlal (misleading them), as one says of the one who leaves the main road: i'tisaf (wandering blindly) or going off into the byways of the road [[His words "in the byways of the road": in al-Sihah it is "in baqiyyat al-tariq," meaning the minor roads that branch off from the main road. (ʿ)]]:

﴿Where are you going?﴾ Their condition is compared to the condition of one who abandons the truth and turns away from it toward falsehood. ﴿لِمَنْ شَاءَ مِنْكُمْ﴾ ("for whoever among you wills") is a substitution (badal) for "the worlds." They were singled out for the substitution because those who willed uprightness by entering Islam are the ones who benefit from the Reminder, so it is as if it was not addressed to anyone else, though it is an admonition to all of them. ﴿وَمَا تَشَاءُونَ﴾ ("and you will not will") uprightness, O you who wish it, except by the enabling (tawfiq) of Allah [[His words "O you who wish it, except by the enabling of Allah": interpreting the will in this way is based on the view that the act of the servant is created by the servant and willed by him, not by the creation of Allah the Exalted nor by His will. Or: ﴿وَمَا تَشَاءُونَ﴾ ("and you will not will") it, you who do not will it except by the compulsion and coercion of Allah.
